clinicalScope: The liver as a normal organ and its common disease spectrum in adult patients presenting to low‑resource East African hospitals.
subject: Anatomy
summary: The liver is the body’s largest gland, sitting under the right rib cage and performing vital metabolic, synthetic and detoxifying tasks. In East African hospitals clinicians must link its anatomy to common problems such as hepatitis, malaria‑related cholestasis and trauma‑related rupture.

sections.p: The liver is a large, wedge‑shaped, intraperitoneal organ that occupies the right hypochondrium, epigastrium and part of the left hypochondrium. It is covered by a fibrous Glisson’s capsule and divided into functional lobes and segments.
b: Right lobe ≈ 60 % of mass; left lobe ≈ 40 %
Caudate and quadrate lobes are defined on the visceral surface
Porta hepatis is the gateway for the portal vein, hepatic artery and bile ducts
Weight 1.2–1.5 kg in adults; can enlarge up to 2 kg in hepatomegaly

sections.p: The liver originates from the foregut endoderm (hepatic diverticulum) around week 3 of gestation and grows into the septum transversum mesenchyme.
b: Hepatoblasts differentiate into hepatocytes and Kupffer cells
Umbilical vein becomes the ligamentum teres; its remnant lies in the falciform ligament
Failure of regression can produce a patent para‑umbilical vein (rare)
Congenital biliary atresia stems from abnormal ductal plate remodeling

sections.p: The liver rests on the diaphragm and is in close contact with the stomach, duodenum, right kidney and right adrenal gland.
b: Diaphragmatic surface: smooth, convex, contacts diaphragm
Visceral surface: irregular, molded by stomach, duodenum, colon, right kidney
Falciform ligament attaches liver to anterior abdominal wall and contains ligamentum teres
Coronary and triangular ligaments anchor the liver to the diaphragm

sections.p: Dual inflow: portal vein (75‑80 %) and hepatic artery (20‑25 %). Outflow via three hepatic veins into the inferior vena cava.
b: Portal vein delivers nutrient‑rich, deoxygenated blood from GI tract
Hepatic artery supplies oxygenated blood; important in cirrhosis where portal flow falls
Right, middle and left hepatic veins drain the liver centrally
In low‑resource settings, Doppler ultrasound is the main tool to assess flow

sections.p: Sensory innervation comes from the hepatic plexus (phrenic and vagus). Lymph drains to hepatic, celiac and pericaval nodes.
b: Visceral pain is poorly localized, felt in right shoulder (phrenic C3‑C5)
Parasympathetic vagal fibers modulate bile secretion
Lymphatics follow the portal triad to the hepatic nodes
Palpable tender liver edge may indicate capsular stretch or inflammation

sections.p: The liver is composed of hexagonal lobules centered on a central vein, radiating portal triads, hepatocytes, Kupffer cells and a sinusoidal network.
b: Hepatocytes perform metabolism, protein synthesis and detoxification
Kupffer cells are resident macrophages that clear bacteria and debris
Sinusoids lack a basement membrane, allowing plasma‑protein exchange
Space of Disse contains stellate cells that store vitamin A and become fibrogenic

sections.p: Key roles include carbohydrate homeostasis, protein synthesis, bile production, drug metabolism and immune filtration.
b: Glycogenolysis provides glucose in early fasting; gluconeogenesis dominates after 12 h
Urea cycle converts ammonia to urea; failure leads to hepatic encephalopathy
Cytochrome P450 enzymes (e.g., CYP3A4) metabolise most oral drugs – first‑pass effect
Bile acids emulsify dietary fats; obstruction causes cholestasis

sections.p: Understanding segmental anatomy guides surgical resection and percutaneous drainage; portal‑vein flow informs prognosis in hepatitis and malaria‑related liver injury.
b: Couinaud segments (I‑VIII) are defined by portal and hepatic vein branches
Right‑upper quadrant pain with a palpable liver edge suggests hepatomegaly from viral hepatitis or malaria
Tenderness over the liver capsule after blunt trauma raises suspicion of laceration
In malaria, sequestration of parasitized erythrocytes can cause transient hepatomegaly and jaundice

sections.p: Frequent liver problems in low‑resource East Africa include viral hepatitis (B & C), malaria‑associated cholestasis, aflatoxin‑induced injury, trauma, and schistosomal periportal fibrosis.
b: Acute viral hepatitis: fever, right‑upper‑quadrant pain, jaundice, ALT > 500 U/L
Malaria‑related cholestasis: conjugated bilirubin rise, mild transaminase rise, often with fever
Blunt abdominal trauma: hepatic laceration, may present with hypotension and peritoneal signs
Schistosoma mansoni: periportal “pipe‑stem” fibrosis, portal hypertension, splenomegaly

sections.p: Physical exam and bedside ultrasound are the mainstays where CT/MRI are scarce.

t.b: Detects hepatomegaly, tenderness, capsular stretch – a liver edge > 2 cm below the costal margin is abnormal
Answers: Is there free intra‑abdominal fluid? Positive fluid in Morison’s pouch suggests hepatic bleed
Answers: Size, echotexture, focal lesions, portal vein diameter. A bright, coarse pattern suggests chronic hepatitis or fibrosis
Answers: Hepatocellular injury (ALT/AST > 2 × ULN), cholestasis (ALP > 250 U/L, GGT > 100 U/L), synthetic function (INR > 1.5 indicates decompensation)

sections.p: Anatomical variants affect surgical planning and interpretation of imaging.
b: Accessory right hepatic lobe may mimic a mass on plain X‑ray
Absent or replaced right hepatic artery (from SMA) occurs in ~10 % of people
Congenital absence of the left hepatic vein is rare but can cause segmental congestion
Persistent ductus venosus can lead to portal‑systemic shunting

sections.p: A systematic bedside method ensures no key clue is missed, especially when investigations are limited.
b: History: travel, malaria prophylaxis, hepatitis vaccination, alcohol, herbal medicines, trauma
Examination: inspect for jaundice, palpate liver edge, assess for ascites (shifting dullness), check for hepatic encephalopathy (asterixis)
Point‑of‑care ultrasound: assess size, fluid, focal lesions
If LFTs unavailable, use bedside bilirubin dipstick and prothrombin time (PT) as surrogate for synthetic function

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe right‑upper‑quadrant pain with hypotension (possible hepatic rupture)
New onset confusion with asterixis and INR > 1.5 (acute liver failure)
Jaundice with fever, rigors and abdominal tenderness (possible septic cholangitis)
Rapidly rising bilirubin > 10 mg/dL in a malaria patient (severe cholestasis)

faq.q: Why does malaria cause a transient rise in liver enzymes?
faq.a: Plasmodium‑infected red cells sequester in hepatic sinusoids, causing mild hepatocellular injury and cholestasis that usually resolves with treatment.

faq.q: Can a normal ultrasound rule out early hepatitis?
faq.a: No. Early viral hepatitis may have a normal scan; LFTs and viral serology are required for diagnosis.

faq.q: What is the significance of a “nutmeg” liver on cut surface?
faq.a: It indicates chronic passive congestion, usually from right‑sided heart failure, and helps differentiate cardiac from primary hepatic disease.

exam: A 28‑year‑old farmer with fever, right‑upper‑quadrant pain and bilirubin 8 mg/dL – what is the most likely diagnosis and which bedside test would confirm it? — Likely malaria‑related cholestasis; bedside ultrasound showing hepatomegaly and no biliary obstruction supports it.

A patient presents with a tender liver edge 4 cm below the costal margin, INR 1.8, and no trauma – what are the top three differential diagnoses in this setting? — Acute viral hepatitis, severe malaria, aflatoxin‑induced acute liver injury.

In a resource‑limited hospital, how would you assess for portal hypertension without endoscopy? — Look for splenomegaly, thrombocytopenia (< 150 × 10⁹/L), and ultrasound evidence of portal vein diameter > 13 mm.

A blunt abdominal trauma patient is hypotensive; FAST shows fluid in Morison’s pouch – what is your next immediate step? — Activate massive transfusion protocol and arrange urgent laparotomy or interventional radiology if available.

Why is the prothrombin time (PT) more reliable than ALT for gauging severity of chronic liver disease? — PT reflects synthetic function of clotting factors; ALT rises only with acute hepatocyte injury.

A 45‑year‑old with chronic hepatitis B has a liver span of 18 cm on exam – what imaging modality is most appropriate to screen for hepatocellular carcinoma in a low‑resource setting? — Abdominal ultrasound performed every 6 months.

Explain how the Couinaud segmental system guides a right hepatectomy. — Segments V–VIII are supplied by the right hepatic artery and drained by the right hepatic vein; resection follows these vascular boundaries.
What clinical sign distinguishes right‑sided heart failure‑related “nutmeg” liver from viral hepatitis? — Presence of peripheral edema, jugular venous distension, and a history of cardiac disease.
A patient on long‑term isoniazid therapy develops mild transaminase elevation (ALT 120 U/L). How should you manage it? — Continue therapy if ALT < 5 × ULN and no symptoms; monitor LFTs weekly.

How does aflatoxin exposure increase liver cancer risk, and what preventive measure is feasible in East Africa? — Aflatoxin causes p53 mutations; promoting proper grain storage and using aflatoxin‑binding agents in food are practical interventions.
